content.thinking:
This interactive consensus intervention with slider estimates and corrective feedback stands out for combining strong consensus-messaging effects with acknowledgment of genuine scientific nuance around net-zero, which likely boosts perceived integrity and openness. The interactivity should amplify belief shifts (roughly 1-2.5 points) more than policy attitudes, though the 66% figure on item 3 could inadvertently spotlight disagreement — still, the overall effect seems net positive.

Working through the estimates: trust around +2.4-2.5, distrust around -1.5, funding perceptions modest at +0.8 since consensus doesn't target funding directly, policy role +1.0, institutional trust +0.9, belief +1.8, concern +1.1, general policy +1.0, specific policy +0.7, behavior +0.4, with small donation and newsletter upticks. The key insight is that this arm's framing — that scientific uncertainty is a strength rather than weakness — should hit trust dimensions around competence and openness particularly hard, given the 99% consensus figure signals credibility while the meta-commentary signals institutional honesty.

parsed_output.reasoning_summary: This arm is the classic consensus correction, but strengthened in two ways: it is interactive (respondents guess, then receive corrective feedback, so the surprise of learning 99% vs. their typical underestimate of ~65-75% drives updating), and it frames the existence of disagreement on projections as a normal feature of science, which speaks directly to scientists' openness and integrity rather than just their competence. Mechanistically it targets (a) perceived consensus/competence and (b) belief in human causation most proximally, so I put the multidimensional trust battery near the upper-middle of the expected 0.5-3.5 range (+2.4) and belief_post at +2.0 despite pre-treatment anchoring, consistent with consensus meta-analyses (d ~0.08-0.12 on belief, larger on perceived agreement, which is not measured here). Distrust falls a bit less in absolute magnitude than trust rises, as is typical for the asymmetric distrust item. Funding, policy-role, and institutional trust are only indirectly implicated (the text says nothing about money, advocacy, or agencies), so they get sub-1.5-point effects, with inst_trust further diluted by the federal-government item. Concern and policy support are downstream of belief and get ~0.7-1.2 points; self-reported behavior ~0.45; the incentivized donation and real newsletter sign-up get only a few cents and about one percentage point, per behavioral-megastudy calibration.
